title: Knowledge Check 5: Lessons 21-25
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 21-25 of the ai-power-user series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: What makes a runbook useful to someone other than the person who built the automation?
options: It teaches the entire subject from the very beginning to any reader
It hands a reader with the right background the details in memory
It keeps a full copy of the tool so the reader can rebuild it
It records every version of the automation that has ever run
questions.explanation: A runbook exists so a procedure survives the person who first worked it out. It hands someone with the right background but not your memory the specific details you would otherwise carry in your head.

questions.question: You change a setting in an automation but forget to update its runbook entry. Why does this matter?
options: The runbook entry grows longer than the automation it describes
The edit without a matching entry erases its own documentation
The tool refuses to run again until the entry is corrected by hand
The next reader has to rebuild the automation entirely from scratch
questions.explanation: A change to the workflow without a change to the record leaves the documentation describing an automation that no longer exists. The habit that prevents this is to edit the entry in the same sitting as the automation.

questions.question: While writing a runbook entry you are not sure what triggers an automation, only that it runs most mornings. What should you do?
options: Write down a plausible trigger so the entry looks finished and complete
Leave the trigger section out so the entry stays short and easy to update
Write that the trigger is unknown and then go check it
Remove the automation from your stack since you cannot describe it
questions.explanation: A truthful entry with a gap is a roadmap, while a polished entry with a silent guess is a trap. Recording the unknown and verifying it keeps the record honest and useful.

questions.question: What distinguishes a workflow that is genuinely shared from one that is merely passed along?
options: The builder demonstrates it live to the team at least once
It runs on every teammate's machine with identical settings
A non-builder can run and repair it from the written record alone
It produces exactly the same output as the manual process it replaced
questions.explanation: A shared workflow is one a person who did not build it can run, maintain, and repair using only the written record. Sending a link or giving a live demo is the passed-along move, not sharing.

questions.question: A team is adopting one person's automation. What is the sound sequence for turning it into a shared workflow?
options: Send the whole team the record and the tool link at the same time
Adapt for a stranger, test one second user, then set the data rules
Rewrite the automation in a new tool, then document it for the team
Publish the record first, then find out who happens to use it
questions.explanation: Sharing is a packaging problem: rewrite the record so a stranger can follow it, prove it with one real second user before inviting the rest, and name the ownership and data rules it touches.

questions.question: How does a shared workflow turn into shadow AI?
options: It is shared through a free tool the organization never paid for
Its output differs slightly from the manual process for the same input
It runs on company data with no owner, no version, and no data rules
It is run by more than three people on the same day
questions.explanation: Shadow AI is an AI process running outside approved governance and oversight. Once a workflow touches company data with no named owner, no version, and no rules on what it may read, sharing has become a risk the organization cannot see.

questions.question: A workflow's output changes even though the tool, prompt, and input are all the same. What is this called?
options: A tool update, because the app shipped a new version
A deprecation, because the vendor is retiring a feature
Behavior drift, because the model behind it changed
A data error, because the input files no longer match
questions.explanation: Behavior drift is the same tool, prompt, and input producing different output because the model underneath was swapped. It is silent, and only a saved baseline lets you tell it apart from your own mistake.

questions.question: What is a smoke test in this context?
options: A full rebuild of the workflow to match the newest tool version
Running a known-good input and comparing it to the baseline
Reading the vendor's release notes and status page for each tool
Asking the vendor to confirm whether the underlying model changed
questions.explanation: A smoke test runs a known-good input through the workflow and compares the result to the output you know is correct. A match means the change did not break it; a difference means you caught the break before anyone else did.

questions.question: A minor patch ships for a tool, and a smoke test shows your workflow still returns the expected output. What is the right response?
options: Reword the prompt anyway, since every update should be treated as a reason to change
Ride it out, since a verified change that does not affect output needs no action
Retire the workflow, because any change to a tool is a sign it is no longer worth keeping
Stop running smoke tests, since a passing test means the test is no longer needed
questions.explanation: A change that a smoke test confirms does not affect your workflow needs no action. The discipline is to confirm that with the test rather than assume it, since riding out an unchecked change is neglect.

questions.question: A workflow dies because a data source changed its format. What is the difference between the proximate cause and the root cause here?
options: The format change is proximate; the missing check is the root cause
The missing check is proximate; the format change is the root cause
Both are the format change, since that is the trigger that started the failure
Both are the missing check, since the format change could not be predicted
questions.explanation: The proximate cause is the immediate trigger you cannot control, such as an external format change. The root cause is the underlying condition you can fix, such as the absence of a check that would have caught the empty read.

questions.question: Why should a post-mortem on your own failed workflow stay blameless?
options: Because blaming yourself is against company policy in most teams
Because a conclusion like 'I was careless' names nothing you can fix
Because the workflow's failure is never the builder's responsibility
Because blameless means no one is ever held accountable for a failure
questions.explanation: Blamelessness is about reaching causes you can change. A verdict of personal carelessness explains nothing and fixes nothing, while a system-level cause such as a missing check gives you something concrete to repair.

questions.question: A post-mortem reaches a clear root cause but produces no assigned fixes. Why does this fall short?
options: Because the timeline alone is the real output of a post-mortem
Because action items only matter when a whole team runs the workflow
Because conclusions with no owners and deadlines are a story, not a fix
Because a root cause does not need to be written down once it is understood
questions.explanation: The follow-up actions are the point of the exercise. Without specific fixes carrying owners and deadlines, the review documents what happened but does nothing to stop it from happening again.

questions.question: What does it mean, in plain terms, for a tool to be reliable?
options: It has never suffered a service outage
It comes from the largest and best-known vendor
Its failures can be predicted, tolerated, and recovered from
It advertises the highest uptime percentage on its landing page
questions.explanation: No tool never fails, so reliability is not about avoiding failure. A reliable tool is one whose failure you can predict, tolerate, and recover from, which is a property you can measure and plan around.

questions.question: A vendor promises a specific uptime percentage, but missing it earns only an apology, not a refund or credit. How should you classify that promise?
options: As a service level objective, a target that carries no penalty when missed
As a service level agreement, because it sets a specific number
As a service level indicator, the raw measurement of uptime
As an error budget, the amount of downtime the vendor is allowed
questions.explanation: The test is what happens if the number is missed. A financial penalty makes it an agreement; an apology with no consequence makes it an objective, even when it is advertised with a specific figure.

questions.question: When a vendor's marketing promise and its observed history of incidents disagree, which should guide your decision?
options: The promise, since the vendor knows its own systems best
The track record, because observed behavior is what your future will repeat
Neither, since no vendor's claims can ever be checked
Whichever is more recent, since both can change over time
questions.explanation: Observed behavior over time is the strongest evidence you can have, while a promise is only a hypothesis about the future. When the two disagree, size your dependence on what the tool has actually done, not on what it says it will do.
